patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.confidence_note: The two deaths at Beur in May 2021 are now recorded outside the lender. The Caravan of 15 September 2021 names the dead as Saddam Hussien, 20, and Mohammed Iqbal Hussain, 18, both from Bhagwangola in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, puts them in a sewer at the Namami Gange works in the Beur locality of Patna on 31 May 2021, and gives the chain of employment as BUIDCo to Larsen and Toubro to a Murshidabad subcontractor, Nayan Raza; Maktoob Media of 1 July 2021 reports a fact-finding visit by the Dalit Adivasi Shakti Adhikar Manch and Loktantrik Jan Pahal, which held the company and contractor responsible and said an FIR should have been registered against them, and records that the police instead registered an unnatural-death FIR, number 15/21. The Comptroller and Auditor General's audit of the Namami Gange works in Bihar, for the year ended March 2020, independently names BUIDCo as executing agency and Larsen and Toubro as the firm laying the Beur sewerage network, and records cracks and leaks at the Beur plant on physical verification in January 2021. The Bank's own completion report is what ties these works to the credit. Its investment table lists 'Patna Beur: Sewerage works' and 'Begusarai Sewerage & STP' among the 32 investment contracts the project awarded, the Beur sewerage works still on-going at closing, and its safeguards section places the two 2021 fatal incidents at project sites at Begusarai and Beur and gives the cause as gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice. No outside document read names the World Bank as financier of the Beur sewer: the Caravan attributes the Beur sanction to a Rs 398 crore allocation by the Ministry of Jal Shakti of 6 April 2017, and the Comptroller and Auditor General treats the Bihar works as centrally funded Namami Gange. An Indian court does name the Bank for a different package of this credit: the Patna High Court judgment below records that the invitation for bids stated the National Ganga River Basin Authority had received US$1 billion from the World Bank towards the cost of this project, and asks whether BUIDCo may ignore its arrangements with the Bank on the strength of the state's 30 per cent share of the funding. Two men died, and the two outlets differ over one of the names rather than describing four people. The Caravan's names come from its own reporting in Patna, including an interview with Saddam Hussien's elder brother Nairu Hussein, who was working on the same job; Maktoob Media's come from the two organisations' press note and give Mohamad Idrish for the man the Caravan calls Saddam Hussien. Only Iqbal is common to both, and the difference is not resolved here: two further Indian reports of the same incident would not open. On procurement, the Patna High Court in M/s EMS Infracon Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, CWJC No. 9597 of 2021, decided 19 July 2021, set aside BUIDCo's blacklisting of a bidder for the Munger sewage treatment plant and 167.3 km sewerage network under this credit, found that BUIDCo had "acted irresponsibly in passing the impugned order in casual and cavalier manner", recorded that three blacklisting orders against bidders on the same invitation for bids by the same Chief Engineer had been quashed, and ordered a fresh technical bid evaluation chaired by the Development Commissioner with the Mission's Executive Director (Technical) on the committee. The riverfront resettlement itself is unchanged: the 249 families, the two-year stall in the land allotment, the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid, and the Begusarai death in March 2021 still rest on the Bank's completion report alone. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the Patna riverfront development or on the deaths; the only Ganga-pollution matter that names this programme, M C Mehta v. Union of India before the National Green Tribunal, records neither.

field_changes.killed_note: Three deaths. The Bank's completion report places two fatal incidents in 2021 at project sites at Begusarai, in March, and Beur, in May, killing three labourers, and gives the cause as gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice and negligence on occupational health and safety training; its investment table lists both sites among the project's 32 investment contracts. That tie between the deaths and this credit is the lender's own and is unchanged by this round. What is now recorded outside the lender is the two deaths themselves. The Caravan of 15 September 2021 puts them in a sewer on the Namami Gange works at Beur, Patna, on 31 May 2021, names them as Saddam Hussien, 20, and Mohammed Iqbal Hussain, 18, both from Bhagwangola in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, and traces the work from BUIDCo to Larsen and Toubro to a subcontractor, Nayan Raza. Maktoob Media of 1 July 2021, reporting a fact-finding press note, gives the names as Mohamad Idrish and Mohamad Iqbal and records that the police registered an unnatural-death FIR, 15/21, rather than a culpable homicide case. Two men, one name shared between the accounts; the other name is unresolved. Neither report names the World Bank. The Begusarai death of March 2021 appears in no document outside the Bank's report that was read.

corrections: The completion report says of the three deaths that "the next-of-kin were duly compensated" and, in its risk section, that compensation to the next of kin "were fully paid". For the two Beur deaths that was not true for at least three and a half months: the fact-finding report carried by Maktoob Media on 1 July 2021 says no compensation had been paid, and the Caravan, reporting from Patna on 15 September 2021, says the families had received nothing and that "by mid September, no culpable homicide case had been registered". The completion report of 28 February 2023 may be describing payments made later; it gives no date, and it does not mention that the police registered only an unnatural-death FIR.

The card's place field and its account of the deaths treat Beur as part of the riverfront works. They are separate investments: the completion report's investment table lists 'Patna: River Front Development' and 'Patna Beur: Sewerage works' as different contracts, and the two men died in a sewer on the Beur sewerage network, not at the riverfront.

The card's confidence note says no independent account of the two fatal incidents was found. Two Indian reports carry them: The Caravan of 15 September 2021 and Maktoob Media of 1 July 2021. Neither ties the works to the World Bank.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.what_the_outside_source_settles: That two labourers died in a sewer on the Namami Gange works in Beur, Patna, on 31 May 2021; who they were, where they came from and how old they were; who held the contract and who sublet it; that the police treated the deaths as unnatural deaths rather than as a crime by the company; and that no compensation had reached the families by mid-September 2021. Separately, that the Munger bid evaluation under this credit was defective enough for the Patna High Court to quash the blacklisting of a bidder and order the evaluation done again, and that three blacklisting orders by the same Chief Engineer on the same invitation for bids were found illegal.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.what_it_does_not_settle: Nothing about the riverfront resettlement: no outside document read names the 249 families, the stalled land allotment, the extra cash paid instead of land, or the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled. karnataka-state-highways-ii-compensation.confidence_note: Two outside documents now carry part of this harm. The High Court of Karnataka at Dharwad, on 24 November 2021, decided MFA No. 102520/2017 and 29 connected appeals brought by the Assistant Commissioner (Land Acquisition), Karnataka State Highway Improvement Project, against landowners of Karagudari village, Hangal taluk, Haveri district, whose land was taken under a final notification of 10 January 2011 for the link road between State Highway 1 and State Highway 69 from Hangal to Tadas, Link No. M7D. The Bank's completion report lists M7D Hangal-Tadasa, 43.46 km, as package WEP-2B of this project, awarded as a contract on 6 July 2013 and completed on 31 January 2017, which is what identifies the road; the Karnataka project unit's own package table gives the same road, length and dates under World Bank Loan No. 8022-IN, and dates the first Karnataka highways project to 2001 to 2008, so a final notification of January 2011 cannot belong to the earlier project. The owners went to the reference court at Hangal, which in a common judgment of 2 November 2016 on thirty references fixed the market value at Rs 44,000 per gunta; the state appealed, and the High Court cut it, holding that "market value of the said lands is fixed at Rs.35,000/- per gunta", following a coordinate bench judgment of 20 February 2021 on Nitaginakoppa lands under the same notification. The general award of 30 April 2011 is recorded in the judgment of the coordinate bench's Nitaginakoppa case, not separately for Karagudari; for Karagudari the judgment establishes the same final notification and the same road. Nearly eleven years passed between that notification and the final figure, and the state's appeal lowered what the reference court had allowed by a fifth. Second, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, auditing Karnataka's public sector undertakings for the year ended 31 March 2019, examined the six roads the Karnataka Road Development Corporation built under this loan and found "delay in initiation of land acquisition in respect of six projects": the roads were identified in May 2011 and the loan and project agreements with the IBRD concluded in that month, but the corporation began acquisition only between September 2014 and October 2017, final notifications for possession ran from August 2016 to February 2019, and the Resettlement Action Plan was approved only in 2015. Audit attributed this to the late formation of the land acquisition cell in 2012 and the late engagement of staff in 2014. A third document, Kumaraswamy J R and others v. The Project Director, Project Implementation Unit, KSHIP, WP No. 16880 of 2022, decided 2 January 2023, records three brothers of Jinnagara village, Kunigal taluk, Tumkur district whose land had been acquired under a notification of 28 September 2010 and who had made four representations about compensation between January 2020 and April 2021 that were not considered; the court gave the project three months to decide them once the government furnished information, warning that lapsing officials would be personally liable for costs. It is the brothers' grievance that is recorded, not a finding that compensation was unpaid, and the order does not name the road, so the parcel is not tied to this project beyond the acquiring authority, though the completion report lists links 63C Huliyurdurga-Kunigal and 63D Kunigal-Tumkur among its roads and the project's supervision consultant, URS Scott Wilson India, is a respondent. The rest of the card is unchanged and still rests on the Bank's documents and on the two impact evaluations the project commissioned: the 602 acres and 6,800 landowners, the 2,200 informal occupiers, the 200 households displaced, the income tax deducted from 7 and 67 people's compensation, the 40 per cent of compensation deposited in the courts, and the two named villages. The Comptroller and Auditor General's paragraphs about Rs 180 crore of unpaid compensation and awards delayed 13 to 23 months are about the Yelahanka to Andhra Pradesh border road, which the same chapter treats as a project of the corporation outside the World Bank co-financing, and are not used here: the chapter's Table 5.1.1 lists the six World Bank co-financed projects as WCP-1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, while Yelahanka to the Andhra Pradesh border was approved on a separate viability-gap route through the Department of Economic Affairs and awarded in January 2015 to M/s Ramalingam Construction Company. Appendix-20, which the writer asked a checker to confirm this from, was not downloaded; the chapter itself carries the distinction.

andhra-pradesh-community-forest.confidence_note: Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the evictions. An independent Indian review does carry part of the harm: Working Paper No. 62 of the Centre for Economic and Social Studies, Hyderabad, of October 2004, by V. Ratna Reddy, M. Gopinath Reddy, Velayutham Saravanan, Madhusudana Bandhii and Oliver Springate-Baginski, reviews participatory forest management in Andhra Pradesh and calls the Bank's project the largest single funder of the state's forest protection committees, giving it 2,910 committees against 1,956 under the Employment Assurance Scheme, 918 under NABARD and 411 under centrally sponsored schemes, so rather less than half the committees, and dates the first phase to 1994 to September 2000. On the harm it records, citing Rangachari and Mukherji (2000), the return to the Forest Department of about 24,000 hectares of land that had been under podu cultivation, most of it in the committees of Visakhapatnam and Adilabad districts, and comments that while the department treats this as a success, "land has been taken out of use for livelihood support of tribals". The review does not say which committees that land lay in, so it is a figure for the state's joint forest management as a whole and not a measure of what happened under this credit. It records that in the mainly tribal Paderu division tribal organisations rejected the second-phase community forest management approach for fear of losing more podu land, and that in Paderu villagers felt the department was setting one village against another by granting one village rights over a neighbour's forest on condition that podu cultivation stopped. It distinguishes those who gave up podu land and still had private land to live on from those "facing forced eviction in plain terrain where podu cultivation has almost become permanent cultivation". On numbers it gives, citing Madhusudhan (2003), an estimated 46,725 families who might have been cultivating forestland assigned to the committees anywhere in the state, and separately that the Resettlement Action Plan under this project's second phase provided a rehabilitation grant and livelihood opportunities to an estimated 11,680 families. The two are not a ratio: the first is an estimate of possible cultivators across the state's committees, the second a provision made under this credit. Both are figures the review takes from another author rather than its own field counts, and the review is an academic survey rather than a judgment or an audit, so it does not settle the dispute on the card between Samata's account of coercion and the forest department's account of voluntary departure; it reports both readings itself. What it does put in one place is that dispute, the lender and a count. At pages 61 and 62 it describes a letter from thirteen non-governmental organisations to Edwin R. Lim, the World Bank's Country Director, on tribal rights, podu land and the second-phase project, carrying a 1999 study by Samata in North Coastal Andhra which found that of 1,500 acres of podu land in 29 forest protection committees only 520 acres remained with the people after the committees were formed; the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests condemned the accusations and said there was no coercion of any sort, and his position was that the land had never been the cultivators' in law; and at the Bank's insistence a consultative process on the Resettlement Action Plan was followed, with an assurance that no resettlement would be undertaken in tribal areas until it was complete. The Samata study is the source already on the card rather than an independent check of it. On the judgment route, the only matter Indian Kanoon returns for the project is Divisional Forest Officer, Kothagudem v. Madhusudhan Rao, decided by the Supreme Court on 8 February 2008, which names the Andhra Pradesh Forestry Project only as the source of the funds a forester was charged with embezzling, including Rs 4,865 of unpaid labourers' wages; it records nothing about this card's harm to these people in these forests. The nearest judgment on the facts, Sreeramanjaneyapuram Village Society v. Divisional Forest Officer, Guntur, decided by the Andhra Pradesh High Court on 18 April 2003, dismissed a claim to one hectare each for 400 Banjara, Sugali and Dalit families whose possession of forest land at Venkatayapalem had been formalised through a forest protection committee account that was later cancelled, and recorded the government's case that the members "who encroached upon the forest land, have already been evicted". It is the same scheme and the same state inside the project years, but the judgment names neither the project nor the Bank, and Bellamkonda in Guntur is not one of the tribal forest areas on this card, so it cannot be treated as the same people or the same parcel.

field_changes.displaced_note: No count of evicted families is published. The Bank estimated 28 per cent of people in project areas would be affected and prepared resettlement plans (Down To Earth). An independent review by the Centre for Economic and Social Studies, Hyderabad, in October 2004 gives one figure tied to this credit and two that are not. Tied to it: the Resettlement Action Plan under the second-phase project provided a rehabilitation grant and livelihood opportunities to an estimated 11,680 families, citing Madhusudhan (2003). Not tied to it: an estimated 46,725 families who might have been cultivating forestland assigned to forest protection committees anywhere in the state, from the same author, and about 24,000 hectares of podu land returned to the Forest Department in committee areas, most of it in Visakhapatnam and Adilabad, citing Rangachari and Mukherji (2000) - the Bank's project funded 2,910 of the state's committees out of about 6,200, and the review does not say which committees the hectares lay in. None of the three is a count of families evicted.

corrections: The card says more than 15,000 hectares were taken over in the first phase. The independent review puts at about 24,000 hectares the podu land returned to the Forest Department in forest protection committee areas, citing Rangachari and Mukherji (2000). The two are not rival counts of the same thing: the review's figure covers the state's committees without saying which of them, and the Bank's project funded 2,910 of about 6,200. Neither should be used to correct the other without a document that defines what it counts.
andhra-pradesh-community-forest.what_the_outside_source_settles: That the land under podu cultivation lost to tribal use under Andhra Pradesh's forest protection committee programme was counted in the tens of thousands of hectares, about 24,000 of them in committee areas concentrated in Visakhapatnam and Adilabad, which an Indian academic review reads as land taken out of livelihood use for tribal people against the forest department's reading of it as a success; that a Resettlement Action Plan under this credit's second phase provided for an estimated 11,680 families; and that tribal organisations in the Paderu division refused the second-phase approach for fear of losing more podu land. It also puts the dispute on the card in one document: thirteen organisations wrote to the World Bank's Country Director, Samata's 1999 study of 29 committees in North Coastal Andhra found 520 of 1,500 acres of podu land left with the people, and the state's Principal Chief Conservator of Forests denied coercion. This comes from Indian academic work independent of the lender, though the Samata figures in it are the source already on the card.
andhra-pradesh-community-forest.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the departures were coerced. The review reports both the department's account and the critics' and uses the words voluntary and forced of different groups, so the central dispute on the card stands. It names no family, gives no date for any eviction, gives no compensation figure, and does not say over what period any of its figures run. Its two large numbers - 24,000 hectares and 46,725 families - are for the state's forest protection committee programme as a whole, of which this credit funded under half the committees, so neither can be read as harm under this project. Its Samata figures are not an independent check of the card, because Samata is already the card's source. No judgment, state audit or gazette notice recording an eviction under this project was found.

lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.confidence_note: Everything here still comes from the World Bank's completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. LesothoLII was searched through its API for the works, the places and the parties: 'Nyenye', 'Makhoroana', 'Nyenye-Makhoroana', 'Makhoroana road', 'Mapoteng', 'Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng', 'Senqunyane', 'Integrated Transport Project', 'Ministry of Public Works and Transport', 'Roads Directorate', 'expropriation of land', 'compensation for land', 'compensation for crops', 'resettlement' and 'road construction compensation'. It holds no judgment about these works. The two phrases naming the project's own roads return nothing; 'compensation for crops' returns only section 54 of the Land Act 2010; 'resettlement' returns five documents, the nearest of them a Labour Court case against the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority. The ministry cases that the phrase search does return are about other things: Tsalong v. Principal Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Transport, CIV/APN/398/13, decided 30 October 2017, is a dismissal from the Department of Traffic and Transport after a forensic audit, with no land in it; Nchere v. Roads Directorate, CIV/T/504/19, decided 11 November 2019, is a default judgment of M149,053 for a pedestrian who fell into an unprotected pit beside the main North 1 road near the Mookoli T junction, with no project named and no land, crops or households. The candidate the batch supplied, Ministry of Public Works and Transport and others v. Lesotho Consolidated Civil Contractors (Pty) Ltd, C of A (CIV) 9 of 2014, decided 17 April 2014, is the trap it looks like: it is about the termination on 21 November 2012 of a contract of 18 November 2008 worth M212,771,071.27 for upgrading the road from Likalaneng to Thaba-Tseka, a road that is not on this card, and it mentions no lender, no land, no crops, no households and no resettlement. The harm on this card remains two households resettled, an unnumbered set of farmland strips compensated for bus and taxi bays, culverts that damaged farmland, and a small number of market stalls moved at Makhoroana, all of it the lender's own account, with no resettlement completion report in existence.
